content: The Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF) is a government-controlled organization in Pakistan dedicated to combating the supply and distribution of narcotics, as well as organizing rehabilitation programs for drug users. The ANF is currently led by Director General Lieutenant General Shujaat Zamir Dar. The origins of the ANF trace back to the establishment of the Pakistan Narcotics Board (PNB) in 1957 under the Revenue Division. This was done to fulfill Pakistan's obligations under the International Opium Convention of 1925. The PNB included representatives from provincial governments and federal ministries. Pakistan ratified the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs in 1961 on August 15, 1965. Subsequently, the PNB was renamed the Pakistan Narcotics Control Board (PNCB) in 1973. In December 1991, the Anti-Narcotics Task Force (ANTF) was created, and in February 1995, the PNCB and ANTF were merged to form the ANF, which is now the leading law enforcement agency for narcotics control in Pakistan. The ANF's responsibilities include coordinating efforts among law enforcement agencies to meet international obligations, striving for a drug-free society, and implementing the government's narcotics control objectives. Despite an authorized strength of 2,552 personnel, the ANF currently operates with approximately 1,500 staff members. Other organizations involved in narcotics control include the Airports Security Force, Pakistan Coast Guards, Customs, Provincial Excise and Taxation, Frontier Corps, Frontier Constabulary, Pakistan Rangers, Political Levies/Khasadar Force, Provincial Police, and Pakistan Railways Police. In 1989, the Ministry of Interior established a separate Narcotics Control Division to exclusively handle drug-related matters. A Policy Review Board, headed by the Minister for Narcotics Control and comprising 14 members from relevant federal and provincial ministries, was set up in 1997 to monitor government policies. The ANF's charter of duties includes: 1. Supply Reduction: This involves limiting the smuggling, trafficking, and distribution of narcotics, eradicating opium poppy cultivation, preventing the establishment of heroin laboratories, investigating the assets of drug barons, and pursuing legal cases against offenders. 2. Demand Reduction: This focuses on reducing the demand for illicit drugs through preventive education, treatment, rehabilitation, and harm reduction programs. 3. National and International Coordination: The ANF enhances international cooperation in the fight against drugs and liaises with organizations such as the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), International Narcotics Control Board (INCB), International Police, Narcotics Affairs Section (NAS), Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA), and other foreign anti-narcotics entities. The National Drug Abuse Assessment Study of 2000-2001 highlighted the growing problem of drug abuse in Pakistan. The study, conducted with the assistance of the United Nations Drug Control Programme (UNDCP), estimated the prevalence of hardcore heroin users, including intravenous drug users, and assessed trends in the use of other drugs. Key findings included: Among males aged 15-45 years, there are approximately 500,000 regular heroin users and drug injectors, a rate considered alarmingly high by international standards. Cannabis (marijuana, charas) is the most commonly used drug, followed by heroin, alcohol, and psychotropic substances. Heroin abuse is more prevalent in urban areas, while cannabis use is equally common in rural and urban settings. Heroin users typically have an average of six years of education, with 43% unemployed and 26% in full-time employment. The highest frequency of drug abuse is observed among skilled and unskilled laborers (47%), followed by businesspersons (16%), agricultural workers (5%), and students (3%). Financial support for drug users often comes from casual work (22%), family support (18%), begging (16%), drug peddling (13%), and petty theft (11%). Women account for only 3% of reported drug abuse cases, with psychotropic substances being the most commonly abused drugs among them. The study also revealed that heroin is the drug most responsible for societal unrest, followed by alcohol. Cannabis, while widely used, is not generally perceived as a major cause of social disruption. Among heroin users, 77% reported daily use, while 41% of hashish/charas users reported daily use. Alcohol consumption patterns were more varied, with most users consuming alcohol less than three times a week. A significant proportion of drug abusers are polydrug users, a phenomenon common worldwide. Regarding methods of drug administration, 73% of heroin users smoke or inhale the drug, 11% sniff it, and 15% inject it. Injecting drug use is associated with a high risk of blood-borne infections. Treatment and rehabilitation remain challenging, with 64% of respondents reporting difficulties in accessing treatment. The majority (80%) cited affordability as a major barrier, while 23% pointed to the lack of in-patient facilities in government hospitals. Although 44% of respondents had received treatment for drug problems at some point, most did not receive intensive or sustained therapy. The issue of drug-related imprisonment is also significant, with 35% of respondents having spent time in prison for drug-related offenses. Pakistan has ratified several international conventions and treaties to fulfill its obligations in combating drug trafficking. These include the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs (1961), the United Nations Convention on Psychotropic Substances (1971), and the United Nations Convention against Illicit Trafficking in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (1988). Pakistan has also adopted extradition treaties with 19 countries and directly concluded treaties with several others, including Australia, Iran, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia. Pakistan has taken international initiatives to address drug trafficking, such as hosting the Six Plus Two technical meeting in 2001, the Gulf Cooperation meeting in 2004, and the Paris Pact Expert Roundtable Conference in 2005. Additionally, the government has signed Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) with countries like China, Iran, Russia, Egypt, and Nigeria to strengthen joint efforts in controlling drug trafficking. MOUs with other countries, including Indonesia, Kuwait, and Thailand, are in progress.
